proposals.title: Phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates selective nuclear-import failure before nuclear TDP-43 loss in experimental TDP-43 proteinopathy
proposals.text:
Phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates selective nuclear-import failure before nuclear TDP-43 loss in experimental TDP-43 proteinopathy

In neuron and cell models that express disease-linked TDP-43, phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin NUP98 is hypothesized to be an early intrinsic change in the nuclear pore complex. The phosphorylated pore weakens selective nuclear import. Loss of nuclear TDP-43 and later neuronal dysfunction follow that import failure. NUP98 phosphorylation is hypothesized to be temporally separable from recruitment of transport factors into stress granules. The claim is limited to experimental TDP-43 proteinopathy. C9orf72-linked disease and sporadic ALS are boundary conditions for comparison, and the same sequence is not assumed for every ALS subtype.

Supported premises come only from the packet. Insoluble TDP-43 aggregates associate with nuclear-pore and transport components. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental systems, and related pore pathology is present in ALS tissue [S1]. Those findings support a TDP-43-pore connection. They do not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event or place any such event first in the sequence [S1]. Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA alters RanGAP localization and impairs nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons, and manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms can modify model phenotypes [S2]. This is a genetic-context-specific route to transport failure and does not establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism [S2]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany impaired import, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death [S3]. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulates in those assemblies; that modification is on TDP-43 and is not evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation [S3]. Cellular stress can also sequester transport factors in stress granules and impair transport, and altering stress-granule assembly can modify transport defects and disease-model phenotypes [S4]. Together, [S3] and [S4] document two routes to a similar transport phenotype: granule-independent TDP-43 assemblies and granule-dependent sequestration.

Speculative bridges are explicit assumptions. No supplied source names NUP98, a kinase, or a phospho-site. Unverified prior knowledge, outside this packet, holds that FG-nucleoporins such as NUP98 contribute to the selective barrier and that CDK-family kinases phosphorylate nucleoporins when pores are remodeled in mitosis. The hypothesis assumes that a stress-responsive CDK-family activity places an analogous mark on NUP98 in post-mitotic neurons and that the mark is sufficient to reduce karyopherin-mediated import. The relevant residue is unknown and must be mapped. This bridge is not evidence.

Causal order. The initiating event is increased phosphorylation of NUP98 on assembled pores, preceding measurable loss of nuclear TDP-43. The downstream response is failed selective import, depletion of nuclear TDP-43, growth of cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, and neuronal dysfunction [S1, S3]. Phosphorylation of TDP-43 within those assemblies is interpreted as a later marker [S3]. Stress-granule sequestration of transport factors [S4] and C9orf72-linked RanGAP mislocalization [S2] remain alternative or context-specific routes and are not required steps in the proposed TDP-43 chain. A further alternative is that the phosphate and the import defect are parallel consequences of broader cellular stress, so the two can correlate while the phosphate is unnecessary for the transport failure.

Discriminating test. In human iPSC-derived neurons with a disease-linked TDP-43 variant, and in an inducible cytoplasmic TDP-43 system aligned with [S3], compare isogenic controls across a time course that starts before nuclear TDP-43 loss. Identify the earliest NUP98 phosphosite by mass spectrometry. At physiological expression, introduce a non-phosphorylatable NUP98 allele and a separate phosphomimetic allele at that site, without altering stress-granule scaffolds. In a crossed arm, prevent stress-granule assembly with a perturbation of the type that modifies transport when sequestration is causal [S4], leaving NUP98 intact. At matched time points, quantify NUP98 phosphorylation, nucleoporin localization, a nuclear-import reporter, nuclear versus cytoplasmic TDP-43, transport-factor occupancy of stress granules, and neuronal survival. Add a C9orf72-repeat neuron arm [S2] solely to ask whether the same NUP98 mark is required outside the TDP-43-variant context. The pore-initiation prediction is that non-phosphorylatable NUP98 preserves import and nuclear TDP-43 while stress granules still form and still contain transport factors, and that phosphomimetic NUP98 impairs import in control neurons before cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies appear. The sequestration prediction is that blocking stress granules restores import whether or not the NUP98 phosphosite is occupied. The broader-stress prediction is that NUP98 phosphorylation and import failure rise together while the non-phosphorylatable allele leaves the import defect intact.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is false if NUP98 phosphorylation increases only after import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss, or if non-phosphorylatable NUP98 leaves import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and neuronal dysfunction unchanged while the stress-granule intervention rescues those phenotypes. Failure of phosphomimetic NUP98 to impair import in control neurons at matched expression is a second falsifier.

Limitations. iPSC-neuron timing does not establish the sequence in ALS tissue or in sporadic disease [S1]. Kinase identity and site occupancy stay assumptions until mapping and allele rescue are finished. A phosphomimetic residue copies a regulated phosphate only approximately. The design does not show how pore phosphorylation and stress-granule sequestration would combine in an intact animal, and it does not validate a treatment.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide repurposing to drive uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual oxidative AML blasts
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide repurposing to drive uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual oxidative AML blasts

Hypothesis. In non-APL acute myeloid leukemia, teriflunomide will induce myeloid differentiation and reduce leukemogenic output of cytarabine-residual blasts that retain oxidative metabolism. The proposed mechanism is on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibition with pyrimidine depletion. The intended endpoint is differentiation, kept separate from bulk cytotoxicity and from eradication of ROS-low leukemia stem cells. Teriflunomide is treated here as the active metabolite of leflunomide. Its approval for multiple sclerosis, leflunomide’s approval for rheumatoid arthritis, and assignment of DHODH as the pharmacologic target are unverified prior knowledge and require independent confirmation.

Supported premises. In the specimens studied by Lagadinou and colleagues, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells, which motivates a search for selective metabolic dependencies. That study leaves the therapeutic window of an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor unestablished across AML contexts [S1]. In the cytarabine models of Farge and colleagues, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. Those residual cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and altering that state changed treatment response in the settings tested [S2]. These observations keep residual disease biologically distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population in [S1]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models investigated, linking a metabolic enzyme to a differentiation outcome rather than to nonspecific killing alone [S4]. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is an established comparator that changes leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, in patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up [S3]. That regimen is a mechanistic control. S4 does not establish that every approved drug affecting DHODH reproduces differentiation or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity [S4].

Speculative bridges. The packet does not identify teriflunomide or leflunomide. The first bridge is pharmacological: assumed human DHODH inhibition at exposures used for the approved indication. The second bridge joins [S4] to [S2]. DHODH is mitochondrial and donates electrons to ubiquinone (unverified prior knowledge of enzyme topology). Residual blasts with intact oxidative metabolism [S2] are therefore proposed to remain competent for DHODH-dependent pyrimidine synthesis and susceptible to its blockade, including residual populations that differ from ROS-low, BCL-2-high stem cells [S1]. The third bridge is that a uridine-rescuable maturation program will lower leukemia-initiating activity in that residual context. Genotype or mutation specificity is absent from [S1]–[S4] and is not claimed.

Alternative explanations. Marker shifts could reflect stress or selective loss of immature cells rather than a maturation program. Shared use of the ubiquinone pool could make DHODH blockade phenocopy oxidative-phosphorylation failure [S1], [S3], so energy collapse could mimic differentiation. Fatty-acid-oxidation dependence [S2] could dominate residual-cell survival and leave DHODH irrelevant. Matched normal hematopoietic progenitors could be equally sensitive. Microenvironmental pyrimidine salvage could bypass the enzyme in vivo.

Discriminating preclinical test. Compare primary non-APL AML blasts, including cytarabine-residual samples where available, after separation into ROS-low and ROS-higher fractions. Arms are teriflunomide, a tool DHODH inhibitor of the class studied in [S4], venetoclax as the BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation comparator [S1], [S3], and vehicle, each with and without exogenous uridine. Score separately myeloid differentiation (morphology and maturation markers such as CD11b and CD14), bulk viability and apoptosis, oxidative phosphorylation and respiratory reserve, and leukemia-initiating or long-term culture-initiating activity. Run the same assays on matched normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells. Confirm pathway engagement by dihydroorotate accumulation with UDP and UTP depletion. Anchor concentrations to verified human exposure for the approved indication; until those levels are checked, dose remains an assumption.

Falsifying observation. In this residual oxidative-blast context the hypothesis is disconfirmed if uridine restores pyrimidine nucleotides while differentiation and loss of leukemogenic activity persist; if teriflunomide only suppresses respiration and viability in a venetoclax-like pattern [S3] without a uridine-rescuable maturation program [S4]; if pathway engagement and phenotype appear only above verified clinical exposure; or if normal hematopoietic progenitors lose clonogenicity at the same concentrations that differentiate AML blasts.

Limitations. [S1]–[S4] do not demonstrate clinical efficacy of teriflunomide. Approval, indication, protein binding, half-life, and steady-state exposure need verification outside this packet. Cytopenias and hepatotoxicity reported for approved DHODH-inhibitor use are unverified prior knowledge and mark a marrow-selectivity risk. Nucleoside salvage, lineage bias, and genetic heterogeneity may restrict activity. This design does not set a clinical dose, a combination schedule, or a claim of superiority over existing differentiation therapy or venetoclax-based treatment.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide repurposing — an approved multiple-sclerosis drug used as a DHODH inhibitor to force myeloid differentiation of oxidative-metabolism-dependent AML cells and cytarabine-resistant residual disease
proposals.text:
TITLE: Teriflunomide repurposing — an approved multiple-sclerosis drug used as a DHODH inhibitor to force myeloid differentiation of oxidative-metabolism-dependent AML cells and cytarabine-resistant residual disease.

HYPOTHESIS. Teriflunomide (recalled: approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; its parent leflunomide approved for rheumatoid arthritis; both facts require verification under packet boundaries) achieves systemic exposure of its active metabolite A77 1726 sufficient to partially inhibit DHODH in AML marrow. Because DHODH activity couples de novo pyrimidine synthesis to the mitochondrial coenzyme-Q/electron-transport node, the drug should simultaneously (a) induce myeloid differentiation of AML blasts, as shown for DHODH inhibition generically in S4, and (b) impair oxidative-metabolism-dependent quiescent leukemia stem cells (S1) and cytarabine-resistant residual cells with oxidative and fatty-acid-oxidation features (S2).

SUPPORTED PREMISES (from the packet). (1) S1: ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSCs depend on oxidative phosphorylation and are vulnerable when this metabolism is targeted. (2) S2: chemotherapy-surviving AML cells are not necessarily the LSC population, yet require oxidative metabolism; altering that state changes treatment response. (3) S4: DHODH inhibition drives myeloid differentiation, establishing differentiation as a drug-reachable metabolic outcome distinct from nonspecific killing. (4) S3: venetoclax-azacitidine establishes that metabolic perturbation can reach LSC energy metabolism in patients; it is used here only as the mechanistic comparator, since that combination is an established AML regimen and is NOT the repurposing proposal.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (labeled assumptions). (i) Teriflunomide/A77 1726 is a clinically used DHODH inhibitor and DHODH donates electrons to coenzyme Q in the inner mitochondrial membrane — both are general biochemistry/pharmacology recalled from outside the packet and must be verified. (ii) Achievable clinical exposures suppress marrow DHODH enough for differentiation without prohibitive host toxicity; the free fraction is uncertain because of recalled high protein binding. (iii) The coenzyme-Q linkage means a "differentiation drug" could hit the OXPHOS-high states of S1/S2; the packet itself does not demonstrate this. (iv) Brequinar, an investigational DHODH inhibitor reportedly tested in AML (recalled, unverified), would be a positive mechanistic control but lacks the approved-drug property.

SELECTIVITY AND TRANSLATIONAL LIMITATIONS. Normal hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells also rely on oxidative metabolism, and S1 explicitly warns that not every mitochondrial inhibitor has a therapeutic window. Sustained DHODH inhibition causes immunosuppression and recalled teratogenic risk, limiting exposure. S4's models are experimental; no clinical efficacy is implied. Pyrimidine-starvation cytotoxicity could masquerade as a differentiation benefit unless proliferation and maturation readouts are separated. APL or TP53-mutant contexts may not obey this logic.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Effects could be off-target (A77 1726 has recalled, unverified off-target kinase effects); apparent differentiation could reflect selective survival of mature cells rather than induced maturation; any benefit in residual disease could come from generic respiratory impairment unrelated to DHODH, which would look identical with an unrelated complex inhibitor.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL STRATEGY. Stage 1, on-target engagement: treat primary AML blasts and S2-style cytarabine-residual populations; measure dihydroorotate accumulation and de novo pyrimidine flux by isotope tracing; test uridine rescue of proliferation. Stage 2, outcome discrimination: flow and single-cell CD11b/CD14/CD16 induction, morphology, serial replating, and xenograft limiting-dilution LSC frequency; use uridine to separate the pyrimidine-depletion arm from the differentiation arm. Stage 3, population mapping: assess responses separately in ROS-low/BCL-2-high (S1-like) versus OXPHOS-high residual (S2-like) fractions to test whether the coenzyme-Q bridge is real. Stage 4, selectivity and benchmark: compare normal CD34+ cord-blood/mobilized progenitor colony formation with AML sensitivity, and benchmark LSC depletion against venetoclax-azacitidine in matched PDX models (S3 comparator only).

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION. If teriflunomide at free concentrations matching or exceeding clinically achievable exposure shows clear DHODH engagement (dihydroorotate accumulation, reduced pyrimidine flux) yet induces no maturation markers and does not reduce functional LSC frequency in primary AML or PDX models, and if normal CD34+ progenitors are at least as sensitive as AML blasts (no therapeutic window), the drug–mechanism–context relationship is disconfirmed. Dihydroorotate accumulation without any phenotypic outcome would specifically show that DHODH inhibition is insufficient in this context, breaking the bridge from S4 to teriflunomide.

LIMITATIONS. This proposal is packet-constrained, preclinical, and mechanism-first. All approval status, original indication, exposure, and off-target claims about teriflunomide, leflunomide, and brequinar are unverified prior knowledge requiring explicit checking; the packet provides the AML mechanistic premises only.

proposals.title: DHODH-Dependent Differentiation of Pyrimidine-Salvage-Limited Residual AML with Teriflunomide
proposals.text:
DHODH-Dependent Differentiation of Pyrimidine-Salvage-Limited Residual AML with Teriflunomide

Hypothesis. In post-cytarabine residual AML with high oxidative metabolism and limited pyrimidine-salvage capacity, teriflunomide will induce durable myeloid differentiation through DHODH-dependent pyrimidine depletion, reducing leukemia-propagating capacity at exposures that spare normal hematopoietic progenitors. This proposes a phenotype-restricted repurposing opportunity, not universal AML activity or a claim of previously undiscovered drug–AML effects.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated features in the investigated models, but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. These findings justify testing differentiation in metabolically characterized residual disease; they do not establish that oxidative metabolism predicts DHODH dependence. BCL-2-associated oxidative-phosphorylation dependence in functionally defined, frequently ROS-low leukemia stem cells provides additional motivation for metabolic targeting, without establishing a therapeutic window for another agent [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is an established metabolic comparator, not the proposed repurposing discovery [S3].

Unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide is recalled to be approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and to inhibit DHODH, an enzyme supporting de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Extracellular uridine is recalled to permit bypass through pyrimidine salvage. These drug, indication, and biochemical facts are outside the packet and require independent confirmation before implementation. No approved-dose marrow exposure or AML-selective concentration is established here.

Speculative bridges. The central assumption is that some oxidative residual AML populations remain dependent on de novo pyrimidine production because salvage cannot meet their requirements. A second assumption is that partial depletion releases a differentiation blockade before causing generalized injury. A third is that normal progenitors possess a sufficient functional margin at clinically attainable exposure. None follows automatically from [S2] or [S4]. Low salvage must therefore be measured rather than inferred from oxygen consumption, stem-cell markers, or treatment resistance.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Obtain paired pretreatment and post-cytarabine patient-derived AML populations across independent donors, retaining matched untreated controls. Measure oxygen consumption, de novo-versus-salvage pyrimidine flux, and nucleotide pools before drug exposure. Prespecify oxidative, low-salvage residual cells as the primary context; include oxidative, high-salvage cells and nonoxidative residual cells as biological comparators. Establish concentration ceilings using verified human unbound pharmacokinetics and measured marrow exposure, rather than nominal culture concentrations. Test protein-adjusted exposures in stromal coculture alongside normal marrow CD34-positive cells, including resting and proliferation-matched conditions.

Measure biochemical DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion before assessing maturation, early apoptosis, and proliferation. Require concordant morphology and differentiation-marker changes in genotype-confirmed leukemic cells, not merely expansion of contaminating normal cells. After washout, assess persistence of maturation, clonogenic output, and limiting-dilution leukemia propagation using equal viable leukemic-cell inputs. Reduced bulk viability alone does not demonstrate differentiation or stem-cell depletion. Include vehicle, an independently validated DHODH inhibitor, genetic DHODH suppression, and venetoclax–azacitidine as comparators. Test uridine rescue after demonstrating salvage uptake; where technically achievable, use a biochemically validated, catalytically functional teriflunomide-resistant DHODH rescue to strengthen target attribution.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation could reflect preferential killing of immature cells, nonspecific mitochondrial injury, proliferation differences, or stromal effects. Time-resolved tracking of initially immature leukemic cells and target-rescue experiments distinguish these explanations. The mechanistic hypothesis would be falsified if verified DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion at attainable exposure fail to induce durable leukemic differentiation in the prespecified context. Persistence of the differentiation effect despite restoration of pyrimidine pools would contradict the proposed mediator. Equivalent impairment of normal progenitor function would falsify the proposed selective window even if AML differentiation occurred.

Limitations. Donor heterogeneity, culture-dependent salvage, marrow nutrient availability, and transplantation artifacts may restrict interpretation. Approval records, pharmacology, protein binding, marrow distribution, and systemic toxicity require verification. Positive preclinical findings would support further investigation, not establish clinical efficacy or justify off-label treatment.

proposals.title: Nup98 phosphorylation initiates selective nuclear-import failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons before transport-factor sequestration
proposals.text:
Nup98 phosphorylation initiates selective nuclear-import failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons before transport-factor sequestration

This proposal advances one testable hypothesis. In spinal motor neurons with TDP-43 proteinopathy, phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 inside assembled nuclear pore complexes initiates selective nuclear-import failure. Depletion of nuclear TDP-43, growth of cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, and sequestration of transport factors are downstream responses. The hypothesis applies to TDP-43 proteinopathy and is tested as a separate question in C9orf72-repeat neurons. A single mechanism for all ALS subtypes is outside the claim.

Supported premises are restricted to the packet. Disease-linked TDP-43 associates with insoluble aggregates that contain nuclear-pore and transport components, disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems, and occurs together with pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Those findings support a connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. They leave the initiating chemistry unidentified and leave open other subtype sequences [S1]. Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA is linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons, and manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modify model phenotypes [S2]. This is a genetic-context-specific route. It supplies no direct nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism and no demonstration that sporadic ALS follows the same route [S2]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and cell death [S3]. Phosphorylated TDP-43 within those assemblies documents a modification of TDP-43, which is separate evidence from nucleoporin phosphorylation [S3]. The perturbations in that study do not establish every physiological ALS trajectory [S3]. Cellular stress recruits transport factors into stress granules and impairs nucleocytoplasmic transport, and altering stress-granule assembly modifies transport defects and disease-model phenotypes [S4]. Placed beside [S3], that sequestration route shows that conventional stress granules are not required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect [S4].

Speculative bridges are stated as assumptions. The modified subunit is Nup98. A proline-directed kinase that becomes active during TDP-43 pathology phosphorylates Nup98. The residues are unknown until they are mapped in the same motor neurons. Phosphorylated Nup98 binds nuclear transport receptors less effectively, and selective NLS-cargo import slows. Unverified prior knowledge from outside the packet is that phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporins can remodel pores during mitosis in non-neuronal cells. Using that analogy for post-mitotic ALS motor neurons is speculative. [S1] through [S4] do not name a kinase, a residue, or a Nup98 interaction.

Alternative explanations are tested alongside the hypothesis. A sequestration explanation holds that stress granules capture transport factors and thereby impair import [S4]. In that account, Nup98 phosphorylation is a coincident stress mark. A de-mixing explanation holds that cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies inhibit import and deplete nuclear TDP-43 without conventional stress granules [S3]. A secondary-injury explanation holds that nucleoporin mislocalization [S1] and RanGAP mislocalization [S2] follow broader cellular stress, so phosphorylation appears after transport has already failed. A genotype-restricted explanation holds that C9orf72 repeat RNA and RanGAP redistribution [S2] impair import through a route that leaves Nup98 unmodified.

The discriminating preclinical test uses order of appearance and reciprocal perturbation in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons. Isogenic TDP-43 proteinopathy cultures, C9orf72-repeat cultures, and matched controls are sampled from the earliest inducible window through the start of neuronal death. Measured events are Nup98 phosphorylation on isolated nuclear envelopes, the rate of NLS-reporter import, RanGAP localization, the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio of TDP-43, G3BP1-positive stress granules, and localization of importins and Ran. Candidate residues are mapped by phosphoproteomics in these neurons before genome editing. Phospho-deficient Nup98, altered only at mapped sites, tests necessity inside the disease models. Phospho-mimetic Nup98 introduced into control neurons tests sufficiency without a disease transgene. An orthogonal block of stress-granule assembly tests the sequestration explanation [S4]. Support for initiation requires three observations: phospho-Nup98 appears before NLS-import failure and before G3BP1 granules; phospho-deficient Nup98 preserves NLS import and nuclear TDP-43; and phospho-mimetic Nup98 impairs import in control neurons that still lack stress granules. Support for sequestration is restoration of import by the stress-granule block while Nup98 phosphorylation stays high [S4]. Support for the de-mixing route is import failure that continues to follow cytoplasmic TDP-43 after Nup98 phosphorylation is prevented [S3].

Falsifying observation. In the TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons, the hypothesis is false if NLS-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 depletion occur without an increase in phosphorylation at the mapped Nup98 sites. It is also false if a stress-granule block or a cytoplasmic-assembly intervention restores import and nuclear TDP-43 while phospho-deficient Nup98 does not. An effect present only in C9orf72-repeat neurons would limit the claim to that genotype [S2].

Limitations. Kinase identity, residue choice, and selection of Nup98 remain assumptions. Phosphomimetic alleles approximate regulated phosphorylation. iPSC motor neurons omit aging, glia, and neuromuscular circuits. The packet does not validate this mechanism or any treatment.

proposals.title: CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in sporadic ALS motor neurons
proposals.text:
CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in sporadic ALS motor neurons

Hypothesis. In C9orf72-expansion-negative, sporadic-ALS-derived motor neurons that initially retain nuclear TDP-43, stress-induced CDK1 phosphorylation of NUP98 reduces its residence at nuclear pores. This intrinsic pore alteration initiates nuclear-import failure, causing nuclear TDP-43 depletion and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. “Initiates” means a proximal trigger of transport failure in this defined context, not the first cause of ALS. Unverified prior knowledge motivates the NUP98/CDK1 nomination; the supplied packet provides no evidence for this pair or a particular phosphorylation site.

Supported premises. TDP-43 pathology can disrupt nucleoporin localization and nucleocytoplasmic transport [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can inhibit import and accompany nuclear TDP-43 depletion and cell death without conventional stress granules [S3]. Separately, stress granules can sequester transport factors and impair transport [S4]. C9orf72-repeat models demonstrate another route involving altered RanGAP localization and impaired import [S2]. These findings establish transport vulnerability and competing causal routes, but none establishes nucleoporin phosphorylation as an initiating ALS mechanism.

Speculative bridges. The proposed chain requires CDK1 activity to increase before import failure, directly phosphorylate pore-associated NUP98, and weaken its pore retention sufficiently to impair transport. It further assumes that resulting nuclear TDP-43 depletion contributes to functional decline, rather than merely marking injury. Later cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could amplify transport failure through the mechanisms described in [S1] and [S3]. This feedback is compatible with phosphorylation being upstream initially but downstream during later degeneration; temporal ordering alone would not establish causality.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Study motor neurons from several independent sporadic-ALS donors and matched unaffected donors, using within-line isogenic perturbations. Follow initially transport-intact neurons during maturation and a calibrated, transient sublethal stress challenge. Serially measure nuclear-import kinetics, endogenous TDP-43 nuclear-to-cytoplasmic distribution, NUP98 pore residence, conventional stress granules, granule-independent TDP-43 assemblies, transport-factor localization, and later evoked firing and survival. Measure export, passive nuclear permeability, cellular energy status, and general stress responses to distinguish import impairment from nonspecific cellular collapse.

First, use endogenous phosphoproteomics in matched cultures to identify NUP98 sites whose phosphorylation rises before pore displacement and import failure. Test whether acute CDK1 suppression prevents these changes and whether purified CDK1 directly phosphorylates the same sites. Freeze the candidate site set before independent validation; absence of an early, directly CDK1-dependent signal would count against the proposed mechanism rather than justify an unrestricted kinase search. Then introduce an inducible, endogenous-level phospho-resistant NUP98 replacement after neuronal differentiation, alongside matched wild-type replacement and wild-type reversion controls. Confirm equivalent baseline abundance, pore incorporation, transport, and neuronal health. Protection must accompany verified suppression of the nominated phosphorylation, not simply reduced stress or altered differentiation.

Test the competing sequestration explanation factorially by blocking NUP98 phosphorylation with or without suppression of conventional stress-granule assembly. Continue measuring granule-independent TDP-43 assemblies because eliminating conventional granules cannot exclude the route in [S3]. Rescue of early import by phospho-resistant NUP98 at comparable initial stress and assembly burden would favor intrinsic pore alteration. Conversely, rescue confined to preventing factor sequestration would favor that alternative. To test the proposed downstream mediator, an independently validated, near-endogenous nuclear-retention TDP-43 intervention should improve neuronal function without correcting NUP98 phosphorylation; otherwise nuclear depletion remains an associated readout rather than a demonstrated mediator.

Falsification and limitations. The central causal claim would be falsified if blocking the nominated NUP98 phosphorylation before onset, while preserving baseline pore incorporation, leaves early import failure and subsequent nuclear TDP-43 depletion unchanged. Phosphorylation consistently appearing only after import failure would additionally contradict its proposed initiating role. Donor heterogeneity, neuronal immaturity, stress-challenge artifacts, and structural effects of phospho-resistant substitutions limit interpretation. Even a positive result would support this mechanism only in the tested sporadic-ALS context, not establish a universal ALS pathway or a validated treatment.

proposals.title: Nup98 phosphorylation initiates selective nuclear-import failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons before transport-factor sequestration
proposals.text:
Nup98 phosphorylation initiates selective nuclear-import failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons before transport-factor sequestration

Nup98 is selected as a candidate FG-nucleoporin; the packet contains no nucleoporin-specific or phosphorylation evidence. In spinal motor neurons with TDP-43 proteinopathy, phosphorylation of this pore-incorporated Nup98 is hypothesized to initiate selective nuclear-import failure, with nuclear TDP-43 depletion, cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, and transport-factor sequestration as downstream responses. C9orf72-repeat neurons are a separate test.

Supported premises are limited to the packet. Disease-linked TDP-43 associates with insoluble aggregates containing nuclear-pore and transport components, disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in cell systems, and accompanies pore pathology in ALS tissue; the initiating chemistry remains unidentified [S1]. Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA is linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons, and transport or repeat-RNA manipulations modify phenotypes; this genotype-specific route supplies no phosphorylation mechanism [S2]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport proteins, and accompany impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and cell death; phosphorylated TDP-43 there is a modification of TDP-43 [S3]. Cellular stress recruits transport factors into stress granules and impairs transport, and altering granule assembly modifies phenotypes [S4].

Speculative bridges are assumptions. Unverified prior knowledge holds that Nup98 GLFG repeats bind nuclear transport receptors and that mitotic CDK1 phosphorylates Nup98 at many SP/TP sites, dispersing it and collapsing import and export together. Nup98 is therefore the candidate barrier subunit, with scaffold nucleoporins set aside and Nup62 used as the FG-nucleoporin specificity control. CDK5 is a separate proline-directed candidate assumed for post-mitotic neurons. Reports of Nup98 changes in neurodegeneration lie outside this packet and are unverified prior knowledge. Selectivity assumes limited, substoichiometric phosphorylation at FG-adjacent Nup98 sites that weakens importin-β and transportin binding while Nup98 stays pore-incorporated, so classical NLS and PY-NLS import slow while CRM1 export and passive diffusion continue. High-occupancy phosphorylation that releases Nup98 is the mitotic-like alternative. Testable novelty is the disease-context order and the necessity and sufficiency of limited pore-retained phosphorylation, by mitotic analogy.

Sequestration treats phospho-Nup98 as a coincident stress mark beside granule capture of transport factors [S4]. De-mixing lets cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies inhibit import in the absence of conventional stress granules [S3]. Secondary injury places phosphorylation after transport failure that follows nucleoporin mislocalization [S1] or RanGAP mislocalization [S2]. Genotype restriction confines the import defect to C9orf72 repeat RNA and RanGAP redistribution with unmodified Nup98 [S2]. Mitotic-like collapse removes Nup98 and blocks import and export together.

The discriminating preclinical test orders events and applies reciprocal perturbations in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons. Isogenic TDP-43 proteinopathy cultures, C9orf72-repeat cultures, and matched controls are sampled from the earliest inducible window through the start of neuronal death. Each sample measures Nup98 and Nup62 phosphosite occupancy on nuclear envelopes, pore incorporation of Nup98 versus a scaffold nucleoporin, importin-β and transportin binding to those pore FG-nucleoporins, classical NLS import, PY-NLS import, NES export, passive diffusion, RanGAP, importin, and Ran localization, the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic TDP-43 ratio, G3BP1 granules, and granule-independent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. The dysfunction endpoint is survival to that window plus a nuclear TDP-43-dependent RNA-processing readout. Phosphoproteomics maps sites before editing. Phospho-deficient Nup98 tests necessity; wild-type Nup98 re-expression tests site specificity; phospho-mimetic Nup98 in controls tests sufficiency and is rescued by wild-type Nup98; phospho-deficient Nup62 tests subunit specificity. Pore incorporation and site occupancy are verified on every allele. Arms are a stress-granule block [S4], a TDP-43 allele that keeps nuclear function and blocks persistent cytoplasmic assemblies [S3], and acute CDK1 versus CDK5 inhibition read out by epistasis with phospho-deficient Nup98.

Initiation requires earlier pore-retained phospho-Nup98, selectively weaker Nup98-receptor binding, intact export and diffusion, preservation of import, nuclear TDP-43, survival, and the RNA endpoint by phospho-deficient Nup98, with phospho-deficient Nup62 leaving those endpoints impaired, return of the defect with wild-type Nup98, and mimetic-driven import failure in controls that lack granules and cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. A stress-granule block that restores import while phospho-Nup98 persists supports sequestration [S4]. Import failure that still follows cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies after phosphorylation is prevented supports de-mixing [S3]. Export collapse as Nup98 leaves the pore supports mitotic-like disassembly.

Falsifying observation. In TDP-43 proteinopathy motor neurons the hypothesis is false if NLS-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 depletion occur without increased phosphorylation at the mapped Nup98 sites, if import and export fail together because Nup98 has left the pore, or if the stress-granule block or the assembly-blocking TDP-43 allele restores import, nuclear TDP-43, and the neuronal endpoint while phospho-deficient Nup98 does not. An effect confined to C9orf72-repeat neurons would restrict the claim to that genotype [S2].

Limitations. Kinase identity, sites, partial-occupancy selectivity, and the Nup98 choice remain assumptions. Phosphomimetic alleles approximate regulated phosphorylation, and CDK inhibitors can affect related CDKs, so epistasis with the phospho-deficient allele is required. iPSC motor neurons omit aging, glia, and neuromuscular circuits. The packet does not validate this mechanism or any treatment.

proposals.title: Phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporin NUP98 as an early initiator of nuclear-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss in TDP-43-proteinopathy ALS motor neurons
proposals.text:
Phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporin NUP98 as an early initiator of nuclear-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss in TDP-43-proteinopathy ALS motor neurons

Hypothesis. In spinal motor neurons with TDP-43 proteinopathy, the pattern common in sporadic ALS, phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporin NUP98 is proposed as an early pore-intrinsic initiating event. The untested prediction is that this modification slows facilitated nuclear import, lowers nuclear TDP-43, and promotes further cytoplasmic TDP-43 accumulation while the pore scaffold stays assembled. Later structural pore injury and sequestration of mobile transport factors are treated as downstream amplifiers. The claim covers this TDP-43-proteinopathy context. A shared initiating phosphorylation step for C9orf72 ALS lies outside the claim.

Supported premises. Insoluble TDP-43 associates with nuclear-pore and transport components, and disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in cell systems, with related pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death [S3]. Those phosphorylated species are TDP-43 rather than a nucleoporin [S3]. Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA is linked to RanGAP mislocalization and impaired nuclear import, and changing transport or repeat-RNA mechanisms modifies model phenotypes [S2]. Cellular stress recruits transport factors into stress granules and impairs transport, and changing stress-granule assembly modifies those phenotypes [S4]. [S3] and [S4] supply sequestration routes, and [S3] shows that conventional stress granules are dispensable for some TDP-43-linked defects.

Speculative bridges. Kinase identity, phosphorylated residues, and the choice of NUP98 are assumptions. Unverified prior knowledge, absent from [S1]-[S4], holds that mitotic proline-directed kinases phosphorylate NUP98 within a multisubunit program that disassembles pores, and that FG repeats help set barrier selectivity. Mitotic disassembly is a mismatch for the claimed scaffold-intact import delay. [S1] reports nucleoporin mislocalization and pore pathology. The bridging assumption is that a persistent neuronal stress kinase places a restricted charge on NUP98 FG-repeat sites in pores already assembled in post-mitotic motor neurons. Absent the mitotic scaffold-release program, that restricted charge is proposed to loosen barrier selectivity and delay TDP-43 import while NUP107 and NUP133 stay at the envelope. This phosphorylation-first order is an untested prediction. [S1] and [S3] support the transport and pore associations alone. Phosphorylation is the candidate initiator. Assembly-driven mislocalization is the candidate downstream response.

Alternative explanations. Stress-granule capture of transport factors can impair import when NUP98 phosphorylation is absent or incidental [S4]. Stress-granule-independent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can recruit those factors and block import on their own [S3]. In C9orf72 neurons, RanGAP mislocalization can account for the transport phenotype, with NUP98 phosphorylation a later correlate [S2]. Phosphorylation after failed import, or death from parallel proteostatic stress, would yield the same endpoint.

Discriminating test. Primary cells are human iPSC spinal motor neurons with TARDBP M337V versus isogenic corrected controls. Pre-registered bins are 0, 1, 2, 6, and 12 h after a sublethal sodium arsenite pulse, and only cultures below a pre-specified death threshold are analyzed. Each bin uses pore-fraction mass spectrometry to map NUP98 phosphosites; those sites are outputs and become allele targets only after the map. The same samples score a TDP-43 nuclear-localization-signal reporter, a control SV40-NLS cargo, the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic TDP-43 ratio, G3BP1 granules, TNPO1, RanGAP, and envelope localization of scaffold nucleoporins NUP107 and NUP133. The precedence rule requires NUP98 phosphosite occupancy to rise one bin before either reporter slows, nuclear TDP-43 falls, or TNPO1 is sequestered, with NUP107 and NUP133 still at the envelope. After mapping, near-endogenous phospho-null NUP98 should preserve both reporters and nuclear TDP-43 during arsenite exposure that still forms G3BP1 granules. Phosphomimetic NUP98 in corrected controls, together with G3BP1/2 disruption, should slow both reporters and lower nuclear TDP-43 without granules or sequestration of TNPO1 or RanGAP, while NUP107 and NUP133 stay localized. Matched NUP153 phospho-null and phosphomimetic alleles are the comparator FG-nucleoporin and should lack these effects if the barrier change is NUP98-selective. On phospho-null NUP98, inducible cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies should leave import intact while assemblies remain, favoring a pore-intrinsic step, whereas recovery only after granules disperse would favor sequestration [S4].

Falsifying observation. Falsification in this model is NUP98 occupancy that does not precede import slowing and nuclear TDP-43 loss; envelope loss of NUP107 or NUP133 at first slowing or under phosphomimetic NUP98; unchanged reporters and nuclear TDP-43 after phosphomimetic NUP98 in G3BP1/2-disrupted cells lacking TNPO1 and RanGAP sequestration; a matching NUP153 allele effect; or impaired import on phospho-null NUP98 while assemblies or granules persist. Occupancy rising only after TNPO1 sequestration would mark a downstream correlate.

Limitations. Kinase identity and residue positions stay unknown until the map is complete, and another FG-nucleoporin may be the relevant substrate. Phosphomimetic substitutions approximate charge and can miss kinase-dependent partners. TARDBP M337V and arsenite are protocol choices. iPSC motor neurons omit long aging, glia, and neuromuscular circuitry. A positive result would remain model-specific and would leave the C9orf72 route unresolved [S2]. The design tests a hypothesis.

proposals.title: Salvage-Reserve-Stratified Teriflunomide for DHODH-Dependent Differentiation of Post-Cytarabine Residual AML
proposals.text:
Salvage-Reserve-Stratified Teriflunomide for DHODH-Dependent Differentiation of Post-Cytarabine Residual AML

Hypothesis. In post-cytarabine residual AML whose pyrimidine economy is salvage-limited under physiological uridine, teriflunomide at verified unbound marrow exposure will occupy DHODH, lower UTP and CTP, and produce durable myeloid differentiation with reduced leukemia-propagating frequency, while proliferation-matched normal CD34-positive progenitors retain at least a threefold functional margin. Salvage reserve alone defines enrollment. Oxidative and ROS-low states are interaction covariates. Teriflunomide is recalled, as unverified prior knowledge, as an oral agent approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis and as a DHODH inhibitor; approval, protein binding, half-life, marrow distribution, and labeled safety require primary-source confirmation. A literature search for teriflunomide and leflunomide in AML is required before any drug-level novelty claim. If either agent already induces AML differentiation, the incremental claim is only the locked salvage-reserve contrast. Brequinar is recalled, unverified, as a DHODH inhibitor that has entered AML testing. A quantitative free-exposure and occupancy comparison with its clinical pharmacology is a drug-choice gate: clear inferiority of teriflunomide on unbound marrow exposure, occupancy, and tolerability stops or pivots the agent and leaves the salvage-stratified hypothesis intact.

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]; the packet assigns that result to the pathway, and to other inhibitors, rather than to teriflunomide. Cytarabine-residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and changed response when that state was perturbed [S2]. Those data justify residual disease as the setting and oxidative phenotype as a covariate. They do not show salvage limitation. Often ROS-low, BCL-2-high leukemia stem cells were sensitive to BCL-2 inhibition through reduced oxidative phosphorylation [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine altered leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation metabolism and is an established metabolic comparator [S3]. Repeating that regimen is outside this proposal. [S3] supports stem-cell metabolic effects and does not establish differentiation as its endpoint.

Speculative bridges. No packet evidence shows residual AML to be salvage-limited, or oxidative metabolism to equal de novo pyrimidine demand. The assumptions are that a measurable donor subset cannot refill pyrimidines from physiological uridine, that partial depletion releases differentiation ahead of generalized killing, and that normal progenitors keep the stated margin at the same free exposure. Expression of DHODH, UMPS, and nucleoside transporters versus chemotherapy state is only a plausibility screen.

Operational rules. In a training cohort, lock three metabolic cutoffs with no reference to drug response: de novo-to-salvage isotope-flux ratio at least 3:1, UTP plus CTP at or below 50 percent of the paired pretreatment median, and uridine refill of nucleotide pools below a cutoff taken from that training distribution at physiological uridine. Apply the locked rules to held-out residual donors and paired pretreatment samples. Continue only if at least 20 percent of at least 20 independent residual donors qualify; lower prevalence is a feasibility stop. Durable differentiation means, after 72 hours of exposure and 96 hours of washout at equal viable leukemic input, a concurrent at least twofold rise in CD11b/CD14-positive fraction and mean fluorescence plus a blinded morphologic maturation score in genotype-confirmed leukemic cells, with at least 50 percent reductions in colony output and limiting-dilution propagating frequency. Selectivity fails if proliferation-matched normal CD34 long-term culture-initiating cells or competitive repopulation fall by at least 50 percent, or if the normal-colony IC50 to AML differentiation EC50 ratio is below 3, at protein-adjusted, pharmacokinetics-capped exposure.

Validation. Gate A confirms pharmacology and requires modeled free marrow trough to reach the occupancy linked to differentiation-range pyrimidine depletion, benchmarked against brequinar. Gate B is the locked-cutoff prevalence pilot with salvage-enzyme measurements. Gate C tests held-out salvage-limited versus salvage-replete residual AML and paired pretreatment cells against matched normal CD34 cells in stromal coculture, resting and proliferation-matched, inside the exposure ceiling. Occupancy and nucleotide depletion are recorded before maturation, apoptosis, and proliferation. Comparators are vehicle, an orthogonal DHODH inhibitor, DHODH knockdown, venetoclax–azacitidine [S3], and a fatty-acid-oxidation or complex-I inhibitor matched for viability. Gate D is a patient-derived xenograft with controlled uridine and nutrients, measured plasma and marrow exposure, occupancy-versus-maturation correlation, limiting-dilution propagation, and normal competitive repopulation. Mediator proof requires documented restoration of UTP and CTP by uridine and a catalytically functional teriflunomide-resistant DHODH construct. Time-resolved tracking of initially immature leukemic cells separates maturation from selective loss of immature cells.

Falsification and stops. Biological disconfirmation is verified occupancy and pyrimidine depletion at achievable free exposure without the prespecified maturation and propagation changes; differentiation that persists after documented nucleotide-pool restoration; equal maturation and propagating-frequency effects in held-out salvage-replete cells at matched occupancy; or a fatty-acid-oxidation or complex-I inhibitor matching those effects at equal viability. Feasibility stops, kept separate from mechanism, are prevalence below 20 percent, free trough below the occupancy threshold, or failure to reach marrow exposure. Prior art that already shows the same salvage-stratified result removes the incremental claim.

Limitations. Donor heterogeneity, culture-conditioned salvage, marrow nutrients, and xenograft artifacts limit inference. The cited studies are model- and cohort-specific. Positive preclinical results would justify further study only.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide repurposing for uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual ROS-higher AML blasts
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide repurposing for uridine-rescuable differentiation of cytarabine-residual ROS-higher AML blasts

Hypothesis. In primary non-APL AML, teriflunomide at or below verified unbound Cmax will cause uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation and lower leukemogenic output of cytarabine-residual blasts in a ROS-higher gate, only when that gate has higher baseline dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux than paired ROS-low cells. On-target DHODH inhibition is read out by reduced dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux and UDP/UTP depletion, and is scored apart from bulk kill, fatty-acid-oxidation blockade, and ROS-low stem-cell loss. Teriflunomide is treated as the active metabolite of leflunomide. Multiple-sclerosis approval, leflunomide approval for rheumatoid arthritis, and clinical DHODH targeting are unverified prior knowledge. Numeric free Cmax awaits verification.

Supported premises. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in Lagadinou specimens frequently had low ROS and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells, with the window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor left undefined [S1]. Farge cytarabine-residual cells were inconsistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and changed response when that state was altered [S2]. Those residuals differ from the ROS-low population in [S1], and pyrimidine flux is unmeasured in [S2]. DHODH inhibition in Sykes models promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints, while selectivity of each approved pathway drug stays unshown [S4]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is the established comparator for leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects [S3]. Repeating it lies outside this proposal.

Speculative bridges. The packet omits teriflunomide. Pharmacology assumes DHODH block at approved-indication unbound exposure. Oxidative and fatty-acid features [S2] stand apart from pyrimidine dependence. The proposal is that respiring ROS-higher residual blasts keep mitochondrial DHODH; ubiquinone topology is unverified prior knowledge. Stratum selectivity requires higher baseline dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux in residual ROS-higher cells than in paired ROS-low cells before any drug margin is counted, and uridine-to-UTP labeling stratifies salvage. The context claim is a larger uridine-rescuable drop in leukemia-initiating activity there than in ROS-low stem cells [S1] or treatment-naive bulk. Genotype is unspecified.

Alternative explanations. Marker gains may reflect stress or loss of immature cells. Ubiquinone sharing may collapse respiration in a venetoclax-like pattern [S1], [S3]. Fatty-acid-oxidation dependence may explain residual behavior and leave DHODH irrelevant [S2]. Normal progenitors may be equally sensitive. Marrow uridine may bypass DHODH in vivo.

Discriminating preclinical test. CellROX Deep Red, manufacturer viable-cell protocol, stains 7-AAD-negative CD45-dim blasts for 30 min at 37°C in serum-free medium, read unfixed, before any gate. Dye concordance with [S1] is unverified prior knowledge. ROS-low is the lowest quintile; ROS-higher is above the median (design choices). Cytarabine: 24 h at the sample concentration cutting bulk viability ≥70%, three washes, 48 h recovery, and continuation only if ≥2 million viable blasts remain (smaller yield = technical failure).

Stage 0, drug-free: stop unless residual ROS-higher dihydroorotate-to-orotate flux is ≥1.5× paired ROS-low flux, a design threshold. Median uridine-tracer labeling of UTP pre-declares high- and low-salvage halves. Stage 1 uses only residual ROS-higher cells, teriflunomide ≤ verified free Cmax, ± uridine at verified plasma concentration (~5 µmol/L unverified prior knowledge, replaced when checked). Go: dihydroorotate ≥2× vehicle, UDP+UTP ≤50% of vehicle, uridine restores both to within 20% of vehicle, CD11b+CD14+ rises ≥20 percentage points, and ≥30/100 blinded cells mature. n=12 primary non-APL specimens; paired Wilcoxon, two-sided α=0.05, within salvage half.

A nucleotide go precedes initiating-cell assays. Stage 2 adds strata, normal colonies, and arms ± plasma uridine: teriflunomide; brequinar matched on dihydroorotate within free Cmax (S4-class link unverified prior knowledge); venetoclax [S1], [S3]; etomoxir only if palmitate-supported OCR falls ≥50% and glucose-supported OCR stays within 20% of vehicle (CPT1 engagement unverified prior knowledge). A linear mixed model tests the treatment-by-stratum term on maturation and initiating-cell frequency with salvage half, α=0.05, in stage-0 passers only. Support is a ≥1.5× larger marker gain and initiating-cell drop in residual ROS-higher cells than in paired bulk and ROS-low cells, with CD34+ colonies ≥70% of vehicle. A xenograft of passers, unbound exposure ≤ human free Cmax, is falsified if marrow uridine holds blast UDP+UTP ≥80% of vehicle.

Falsifying observation. Falsifiers are absence of the stage-0 ≥1.5× flux excess; equal maturation by teriflunomide and brequinar in residual ROS-higher, ROS-low, and treatment-naive bulk cells [S4]; a treatment-by-stratum term under 1.5×; uridine restoration of UDP/UTP while differentiation and leukemogenic loss remain; an etomoxir or venetoclax copy without dihydroorotate accumulation and UDP/UTP depletion; concentrations above free Cmax or absent brequinar phenocopy within it; and CD34-positive colonies under 70% of vehicle. High-salvage-only misses are salvage bypass.

Limitations. [S1]–[S4] omit clinical efficacy and marrow selectivity for teriflunomide. Approval, protein binding, half-life, free Cmax, plasma uridine, brequinar potency, and etomoxir selectivity need external verification. Cytopenias and hepatotoxicity described for approved use are unverified prior knowledge and mark marrow and liver risk. n=12 is a yield lock and may underpower the interaction. Salvage, lineage bias, and genotype may restrict activity. Dose, schedule, and superiority claims are deferred.

proposals.title: CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in sporadic ALS motor neurons
proposals.text:
CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in sporadic ALS motor neurons

Hypothesis. In C9orf72-expansion-negative sporadic-ALS-derived motor neurons initially retaining nuclear TDP-43, aberrant CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation weakens pore residence, initiating import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. Initiation denotes a proximal transport trigger, not the first cause of ALS.

Evidence and target rationale. TDP-43 pathology can disrupt pore-component localization and transport [S1]; persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can inhibit import without conventional stress granules [S3]. Stress-granule sequestration supplies another route [S4], while C9orf72 repeats supply a distinct RanGAP-associated route [S2]. None establishes NUP98 phosphorylation as an ALS initiator. Target-specific precedent—CDK1-mediated NUP98 phosphorylation during mitotic pore remodeling—is unverified prior knowledge, not packet evidence. Extrapolation to postmitotic neurons is the central target-selection weakness. The speculative bridges are neuronal CDK1 activation without mitosis, phosphorylation-dependent pore release, and depletion-driven dysfunction. Relevant CDK1 activity must therefore be demonstrated in noncycling motor neurons, excluding cycling contaminants. Unlike the supplied sequestration routes, this proposal begins with intrinsic pore modification.

Temporal and disease-specific test. Use several independent ALS and unaffected donor lines, with within-line isogenic interventions. Longitudinally follow initially import-intact neurons during unstressed maturation; use a calibrated sublethal challenge only secondarily. Predict ALS enrichment of CDK1 activity, NUP98 phosphorylation, and reduced pore residence before import failure or detectable factor sequestration, at comparable energy and stress status. Measure import kinetics, export, passive permeability, TDP-43 localization, both assembly classes, transport-factor capture, firing, and survival. Matched-culture phosphoproteomics identifies early NUP98 sites; orthogonal neuronal CDK1 activity assays, acute genetic suppression, and purified-kinase assays test dependence and direct phosphorylation. Prespecify sites before independent validation.

Phosphorylation-specific causality. Endogenous-level, post-differentiation phospho-resistant replacement, wild-type replacement, and reversion controls test necessity. However, mutation-induced structural protection or broad CDK1 suppression could mimic rescue. Therefore add reversible recruitment of a phosphatase to endogenous NUP98, with catalytic-dead and untargeted controls, confirming loss of nominated phosphates and auditing collateral pore modifications. Conversely, reversible NUP98-targeted recruitment of active CDK1 tests whether phosphorylation produces pore displacement and import failure without preceding sequestration. Reject constructs that alter baseline transport or broadly change stress signaling; artificial sufficiency alone cannot establish disease relevance. Failure to detect early, directly CDK1-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation counts against this target rather than licensing an unrestricted kinase search.

Pore-residence mediation. Add an orthogonal, inducible pore-retention rescue that anchors phosphorylated wild-type NUP98 without reducing its phosphorylation. Include inert-anchor controls and verify normal baseline pore incorporation and permeability. Rescue of early import with unchanged kinase activity, initial stress, and factor-capture burden would support residence as the mediator; phospho-resistant rescue alone would not.

Causal alternatives. Cross NUP98 interventions with conventional stress-granule suppression and, independently, an inducible assembly-deficient TDP-43 replacement at endogenous levels. Validate preserved basal nuclear localization, RNA function, and import, matched initial stress, and reduced transport-factor capture—not merely fewer puncta. Measure effects on NUP98 phosphorylation rather than assuming independence. Import rescue by NUP98 manipulation despite matched early assembly burden favors intrinsic pore alteration. Rescue by assembly suppression while NUP98 phosphorylation and displacement persist favors sequestration; suppression that prevents phosphorylation instead places assemblies upstream. Continued granule-independent monitoring remains essential because conventional granule removal cannot exclude [S3]. These engineered interventions require validation, not presumed selectivity.

Downstream mediation. A separate near-endogenous nuclear-retention TDP-43 intervention should improve firing or survival while NUP98 phosphorylation and reporter-import defects persist. Such rescue supports nuclear depletion as a functional mediator; without it, depletion remains an associated readout rather than a demonstrated causal link.

Falsification and limitations. Verified blockade of the nominated phosphorylation before onset, with preserved baseline pores, that leaves early import failure and nuclear TDP-43 depletion unchanged falsifies its proposed initiating necessity in the tested context. Phosphorylation consistently appearing after import failure also contradicts initiation. Donor heterogeneity, neuronal immaturity, imperfect manipulation specificity, and artificial tethering limit interpretation. Stress-only effects establish conditional vulnerability, not spontaneous ALS initiation; positive findings would remain restricted to the tested sporadic-ALS context, not validate a treatment.

proposals.title: Repurposing teriflunomide as DHODH-targeted differentiation therapy in AML stratified by pre-treatment pyrimidine-dependence biomarkers
proposals.text:
Title: Repurposing teriflunomide as DHODH-targeted differentiation therapy in AML stratified by pre-treatment pyrimidine-dependence biomarkers

Drug and original indication (unverified prior knowledge): I recall that teriflunomide is an approved oral immunomodulator for relapsing multiple sclerosis, inhibiting DHODH and structurally related to leflunomide (rheumatoid arthritis). Approval status, potency, human pharmacokinetics, unbound exposure, and safety (hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, myelosuppression) lie outside the frozen packet and must be verified against regulatory labels before any translational claim.

Novelty positioning (unverified prior knowledge; must be searched and labeled before translation): DHODH inhibition is already an actively pursued investigational AML strategy, including brequinar-based clinical programs, and prior AML studies of teriflunomide or other DHODH inhibitors may exist. The claim here is therefore not discovery of the DHODH–differentiation link, which [S4] establishes. The testable increment is teriflunomide- and biomarker-specific: whether an approved oral DHODH inhibitor achieves on-target engagement and differentiation at clinically modeled unbound exposure despite lower potency, leveraging an existing safety/PK database for rapid translation, and whether a prospectively measurable pre-treatment biomarker identifies responsive patients.

Ex-ante stratified hypothesis: In a pre-specified subset of primary non-APL AML defined before any drug exposure — elevated baseline dihydroorotate-to-UMP pool ratio with low basal UMP/UTP, dominant de novo versus salvage pyrimidine flux by stable-isotope tracing, limited uridine-rescue capacity, and DHODH expression at or above panel median — clinically modeled teriflunomide exposure will cause target engagement, induce myeloid differentiation, and suppress leukemic progenitor activity, while predicted non-responders show significantly weaker effects. Failure of this prospective stratification falsifies the patient-level hypothesis even if the drug works broadly.

Supported premises: [S4] shows DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML and anchors the mechanism, but does not establish that any approved inhibitor reaches suitable exposure. [S1] supports a metabolic dependency of ROS-low, BCL-2-high, OXPHOS-associated leukemia stem-cell populations. [S2] shows cytarabine-resistant residual cells are not necessarily LSC-enriched but carry oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation features; critically, [S2] does not establish de novo pyrimidine dependency in that state, so the residual-disease bridge is speculative and directly tested. [S3] provides venetoclax–azacitidine only as an established metabolic comparator benchmarking readouts, not as a precedent for this repurposing.

Speculative bridges: I assume, as unverified prior biochemical knowledge, that DHODH is a mitochondrial ubiquinone-linked enzyme, so teriflunomide should cause dihydroorotate accumulation with UMP/UTP depletion. The selectivity bridge is that AML blasts and oxidative-state residual cells have less pyrimidine reserve than normal hematopoietic cells, and that differentiation dominates over apoptosis in responsive samples. The [S2] bridge is explicitly mechanistic and unproven: if cytarabine-resistant cells rely on ETC/FAO flux that couples to the ubiquinone-linked DHODH step, uridine rescue of that compartment would demonstrate on-target pyrimidine dependency; failure would sever the bridge.

Preclinical test strategy: (1) Verify approval and PK facts against regulatory labels. (2) In ~20–30 primary non-APL specimens plus healthy CD34+ progenitors and PBMCs, measure baseline DHO/UMP ratio, DHODH expression, de novo/salvage flux, uridine-rescue capacity, and ROS-low fraction ([S1]); classify predicted responders versus non-responders before drug exposure and test predictive value prospectively. (3) Treat with clinically modeled unbound concentrations using pre-registered go/no-go endpoints: ≥5-fold intracellular dihydroorotate rise with ≥50% UMP depletion at ≤3× estimated mean unbound Cmax; ≥2-fold CD11b/CD14 increase with ≥50% CD34/CD117 loss; ≥70% colony-formation reduction; AML-to-CD34+ IC50 selectivity ratio ≥5. (4) Causality: uridine/nucleoside rescue restoring ≥70% of colony endpoints indicates on-target pyrimidine dependency; DHODH knockdown phenocopy, overexpression resistance, and a validated potent DHODH inhibitor comparator. (5) [S2]-informed residual arm: generate cytarabine-resistant residual cells, then measure DHODH engagement, uridine rescuability, matched FAO/ETC flux, and differential sensitivity versus bulk; if DHODH engagement does not affect this compartment or metabolism shifts to salvage, the bridge fails. (6) PDX: ~10 biomarker-classified models, randomized versus vehicle (n=8–10/group), with pre-specified comparisons of marrow blast burden, LSC frequency by limiting-dilution statistics, survival, and normal hematopoietic toxicity, benchmarking differentiation versus the [S3] metabolic-readout framework.

Falsifying outcomes: absence of target engagement at clinically achievable concentrations; target engagement without differentiation or ≥50% colony reduction; effects neither phenocopied by DHODH knockdown nor rescued by uridine (off-target toxicity); AML-to-CD34+ selectivity ratio <2; equal responses in biomarker-positive and biomarker-negative specimens (patient-level biomarker hypothesis falsified); PDX lacking ≥50% LSC-frequency reduction or survival benefit.

Alternative explanations: nonspecific pyrimidine-starvation cytotoxicity rather than differentiation; mitochondrial ETC perturbation independent of DHODH; off-target immunomodulation given the approved immune indication; pyrimidine-salvage rescue or high uridine availability; inadequate teriflunomide exposure relative to brequinar-class potency.

Limitations: [S1] and [S2] are model-dependent and do not guarantee therapeutic windows; [S4] does not show that teriflunomide reproduces DHODH-inhibitor differentiation; [S3] is not transferable to another drug. The biomarker panel is proposed, not validated, and requires multivariate predictive modeling. Teriflunomide potency, long half-life, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity (unverified prior knowledge) constrain translation and mandate exposure-limiting toxicity studies.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide-Induced Differentiation in Pyrimidine-Salvage-Limited, Cytarabine-Persistent AML
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide-Induced Differentiation in Pyrimidine-Salvage-Limited, Cytarabine-Persistent AML

Hypothesis: At clinically attainable unbound exposure, teriflunomide will induce durable myeloid differentiation and reduce clonogenicity in cytarabine-persistent AML with limited uridine-salvage capacity, through DHODH-dependent pyrimidine depletion. Salvage-competent AML and normal hematopoietic progenitors should be less affected. This proposes a context-specific differentiation treatment, not an established AML regimen or universal stem-cell therapy.

Unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, its original indication, and inhibits DHODH, an enzyme involved in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. These drug-specific statements are not established by the supplied packet. Approval details, biochemical selectivity, human unbound exposure, and clinically relevant exposure duration must be checked before translational advancement; no concentration is assumed to be achievable merely because the drug is approved.

Supported premises: DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML systems [S4]. Separately, cytarabine-resistant cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated features but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem-cell population studied in S1 therefore cannot simply be equated with this residual population [S1, S2]. Venetoclax–azacitidine supplies an established metabolism-focused comparator, not evidence that teriflunomide works [S3]. None of these sources establishes teriflunomide efficacy, its proposed salvage-defined selectivity, or acceptable exposure.

Speculative bridge: a subset of cytarabine-persistent AML may retain substantial de novo pyrimidine dependence while having insufficient extracellular-uridine salvage. In that context, teriflunomide-mediated DHODH inhibition could lower pyrimidine availability sufficiently to release the differentiation blockade before causing generalized cell death. Oxidative metabolism is an enrichment feature to examine, not proof of DHODH dependence. The proposed normal-cell advantage is also an assumption: normal progenitors might instead share the dependency.

Discriminating preclinical strategy: study paired pretreatment and cytarabine-persistent primary AML specimens, alongside normal donor hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells. Maintain physiological uridine and protein conditions rather than artificially favoring de novo synthesis. Define salvage-low and salvage-high groups prospectively using labeled-uridine incorporation and complementary de novo flux measurements, with thresholds fixed before examining drug response. Measure oxidative metabolism separately rather than using it as a surrogate for salvage. Test teriflunomide concentration–time profiles constrained by subsequently verified human free-drug exposure.

Establish temporal ordering through direct DHODH activity measurements, pyrimidine-pool measurements, respiration, viability, morphology, and maturation-marker expression. Genotype-confirmed leukemic progeny should acquire mature morphology and lose serial clonogenicity after washout; marker shifts alone are insufficient. Reduced leukemia-initiating activity would require transplantation evidence and must not be inferred from bulk-cell differentiation. Include vehicle, an orthogonal DHODH perturbation, venetoclax–azacitidine, and identically exposed normal progenitors. Uridine supplementation should restore pyrimidine pools and prevent differentiation if depletion mediates the effect. For stronger drug-specific attribution, develop and validate a catalytically competent, teriflunomide-resistant DHODH construct and test whether it rescues both metabolic and differentiation endpoints. Advance responsive specimens into patient-derived models with measured unbound exposure and marrow toxicity.

Alternatives include off-target cytotoxicity, generalized mitochondrial stress, apparent maturation caused by selective survival of pre-existing mature cells, or expansion of contaminating normal cells. Early target engagement, rescue experiments, single-cell lineage tracking, and leukemic-genotype confirmation distinguish these explanations from genuine differentiation.

Falsification and limitations: confirmed DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion at relevant exposure without durable maturation or reduced clonogenicity in prospectively defined salvage-low residual AML would falsify the central prediction. Persistence of differentiation despite successful drug-resistant-DHODH rescue would reject the proposed mechanism. Comparable injury to normal progenitors would falsify the predicted therapeutic selectivity. Marrow metabolite availability, heterogeneous salvage, achievable exposure, and culture-induced state changes may defeat translation. Even successful preclinical results would establish neither clinical benefit nor eradication of every AML stem-cell population.
